idiom_name: Piscina / worker_threads pool with a bounded maxThreads
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no threads in the language; Node runs CPU-bound code on worker_threads, and the official documentation itself says to pool them ('use a pool of Workers ... otherwise, the overhead of creating Workers would likely exceed their benefit'). A pool is a fixed set of Worker instances each awaiting tasks from a shared queue, or a ready-made implementation such as Piscina, which adds a task queue, a bounded maxThreads, run/wait statistics, transfer-list support and cancellation. I/O never needs any of this, because the event loop already interleaves I/O; resources moved to the pool should be things that would otherwise block the loop (hashing, parsing, image work).
pitfalls: Worker threads do not help I/O-bound work: the event loop is already concurrent, and a worker round-trip only adds serialisation.
Creating a Worker per call is thread-per-task with a far higher unit cost (module loading plus a fresh V8 isolate).
Data crosses the boundary by structured clone or transfer: large payloads that are not transferred get copied, and a worker error surfaces as a rejection that must be handled or it leaks the worker.

variants.name: Browser Web Worker pool
variants.idiom_name: fixed array of Worker instances with a Promise-based task dispatcher
variants.implementation_notes: Browsers expose Worker objects but no pool API, so the pool is a fixed array of workers created once from a URL (or Blob), each with an onmessage handler, plus a dispatcher that keeps a queue of tasks and assigns each to an idle worker while resolving one Promise per task. navigator.hardwareConcurrency is the sizing hint. This is the only way to keep heavy computation off the UI thread; because workers have separate globals and messages are structured-cloned, shared state must be rebuilt or transferred inside the worker.
pitfalls: terminate() is the only preemption and it kills the worker with no cooperative stop: recreate the worker afterwards or the pool shrinks silently.
Messages are copied (or transferred), so class instances, DOM nodes and closures do not survive the boundary.
Spawning workers per user action is the thread-per-task anti-pattern and exhausts memory quickly; always cap the pool.
